This method implements a display-only renderer for trained 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes within the Unity engine, optimized for mobile compatibility [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the method implements a display-only renderer for trained 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes within the Unity engine, optimized for mobile compatibility. The evidence confirms: 1) It is implemented in Unity using compute shaders. 2) It uses a specific rendering strategy (sorting, front-parallel quads, specific blending) which constitutes a 'display-only renderer' (it renders the Gaussians but does not mention interactive physics or other non-display features in the context of the renderer itself). 3) It explicitly mentions optimization for mobile, citing 'steady 30 FPS on an iPhone 13' and 'maximum compatibility in mind'. 4) It deals with 'trained' scenes (implied by the export pipeline of Gaussians and embeddings). All facts in the claim are present in the evidence.

It sets itself apart from its siblings by prioritizing maximum compatibility with existing game engine workflows (Mixamo rigging) and mobile stability over the raw performance optimizations found in tiled or sort-free variants [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the method prioritizes compatibility with existing game engine workflows (specifically Mixamo rigging) and mobile stability over raw performance optimizations found in tiled/sort-free variants. The evidence supports this in several ways: 1) It explicitly mentions uploading the mesh to Mixamo for autorigging and exporting to Unity, demonstrating compatibility with these workflows. 2) It describes a 'one-primitive-one-Gaussian' strategy with sorting by z-axis, noting this is important for game engines to handle occlusion, which contrasts with more optimized but potentially less compatible tiled/sort-free approaches. 3) It reports performance metrics (30 FPS on iPhone 13), indicating a focus on mobile stability. The evidence confirms all specific facts mentioned in the claim.

It solves the problem of rendering high-fidelity Gaussian avatars on constrained hardware by relying exclusively on a warped canonical mesh for rigging and using a standard front-to-back alpha blending pipeline [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the method solves the problem of rendering high-fidelity Gaussian avatars on constrained hardware by relying exclusively on a warped canonical mesh for rigging and using a standard front-to-back alpha blending pipeline. The evidence supports this in three ways: 1) It explicitly states 'we made SplattingAvatar solely rely on the warped mesh' for the Unity implementation on mobile devices (constrained hardware). 2) It details the rendering pipeline: sorting by z-axis (front-to-back), drawing front-parallel quads, and using the blend function (ONE, ONE_MINUS_SRC_ALPHA) which corresponds to standard alpha blending. 3) It confirms performance on constrained hardware ('steady 30 FPS on an iPhone 13') and high fidelity ('photorealistic rendering... high-quality details'). All specific facts in the claim are present in the evidence.
